title: Object lifetime: the stack, the heap, and who cleans up
summary: Watch objects being born and dying, allocate on the heap with new and delete, catch a use-after-free with AddressSanitizer, and let std::unique_ptr do the cleanup for you.

quiz.question: Which is the correct order of these lines in the program's output?
options: construct b → construct f-local → destroy b → destroy f-local → construct c
construct b → construct f-local → destroy f-local → destroy b → construct c
construct b → construct f-local → construct c → destroy f-local → destroy b
construct b → construct f-local → construct c → destroy c → destroy b → destroy f-local
explanations: `f-local` lives inside `f`. Its lifetime ends when `f` returns — before control even gets back to the block holding `b`.

Right. A local object is destroyed at the closing `}` of the block it was declared in. `f-local` dies when `f` returns; `b` dies at the end of its inner `{ }` block — before `c` is even created. And when several objects die at the same `}`, they're destroyed in *reverse* order of construction (`c`, then `a`).
`c` isn't created until after the inner block has closed — by then `b` is already gone.
Objects don't wait until the end of `main`. Each local dies at the end of its own scope.

steps.title: Objects you destroy yourself

checks.label: The heap Tracer is destroyed before main ends

hints: `Tracer* h = new Tracer("heap");` creates it; `h->name` reaches a member through the pointer.
`delete h;` destroys it — put it just before the line that prints `main ends`.
On Linux, if you forget `delete`, LeakSanitizer reports a memory leak when the program exits.

steps.title: A use after free

checks.label: dangling.cpp no longer manages memory by hand
checks.failMessage: The output is right — but this step asks you to remove the manual new/delete entirely, so the bug can't come back. Return the string by value.

hints: Read the sanitizer report: *who* freed the memory (the second stack trace) and *who* used it afterwards (the first).
The fix isn't to move the `delete` — it's to stop using the heap here. `std::string make_greeting(const std::string& name)` can just `return "Hello, " + name + "!";`.
Then `print_and_cleanup` has nothing to clean up: make it `void print(const std::string& text)`.

quiz.question: In the original dangling.cpp, what was the root cause of the bug?
options: `new std::string` is slower than a local string.
Nothing in the code said who *owned* the string. `print_and_cleanup` assumed it did and deleted it; `main` assumed it still could use it. Raw pointers can't express ownership.
`std::string` can't be allocated on the heap.
explanations: It is slower, but speed wasn't the bug — the program read freed memory.

Exactly. A raw `T*` says nothing about who must delete it, or when. C++'s answer is to make ownership part of the *type*: values own themselves, `std::unique_ptr<T>` is the single owner of a heap object, and plain references/pointers only *observe*. That's the next step.
Anything can be heap-allocated. The problem was what happened to it afterwards.
`delete[]` is for arrays from `new[]`. A single `new std::string` is correctly paired with `delete` — it was just deleted too early for main.

steps.title: Let the type clean up: std::unique_ptr

checks.label: No manual new/delete left in tracer.cpp
The heap Tracer is destroyed automatically at the end of main

hints: Remove the `delete h;` line — the unique_ptr's destructor does it. Use `h->name` exactly as before.
